summary: Two NASA satellites tally fires differently. MODIS (1 km pixels) misses small fires that VIIRS (375 m) sees, so combining their records creates a false jump in 2012. "Fire Calendar" combines both on a single scale for Haryana and Punjab, India. We count fire spots per month for each satellite, determine how many more VIIRS sees in the years both flew (February 2012 to December 2021), and scale the older MODIS counts by a ratio for each month. VIIRS sees 5.14 times as many fires. Our test shows year-to-year totals are off by about 6.2%, jumping from ×5.15 in 2012 to ×1.02. The result is an estimate, not burned area. The page includes a map of the newest fires and a calendar since
details:
Fire Calendar makes two NASA fire records match. MODIS (older, 1 km squares) and VIIRS (newer, 375 m squares) both spot fires from space, but VIIRS finds more fire spots for the same fires, so joining the records creates a fake jump in 2012. In Haryana and Punjab the raw count goes from 22,810 in 2011 to 126,674 in 2012. Our Python script reads the NASA FIRMS files, counts fire spots per month, finds how many times more VIIRS sees when both sensors worked (5.1 times on average, one ratio for each month of the year), and multiplies the older MODIS counts by that ratio. The website shows 23 years, 2003 to 2025, as one calendar: light yellow for few fire spots, dark red for many.

Now old and new years can be compared fairly. The calendar shows two fire seasons, October to November (64% of fire spots) and April to May (29%), which match the crop harvests, so people can see when burning happens and how it changes. We built it with Python and pandas for the harmonization, and HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Chart.js for the page, with help from an AI assistant (Claude). The page talks to Python, so you can type your own area and get a new calendar. We were honest about limits: the fix is a simple estimate, off by about 6% in our test, and clouds and tiny fires are missed.
